## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a21-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- a21-ideas:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Dependence is a ratio</dt><dd>Net imports ÷ primary energy: 40.0% for Prairieland; its value depends on how primary energy is counted.</dd><dt>Concentration is separate</dt><dd>Coal is 0% imported, yet all of it comes from one county; 31.0% of primary energy passes one strait.</dd><dt>The scarcest input sets output</dt><dd>Graphite (anodes) limits the factory to 23% of its output during the restriction.</dd><dt>Whose money</dt><dd>A price spike sends money abroad for imports and moves money at home between users and producers.</dd><dt>Shocks overlap</dt><dd>A restriction and a fire together cost 18.5 GWh of cells, not 24.5 GWh.</dd></dl>
<!-- a21-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The measures, in symbols</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

$$\text{import dependence} = \frac{\text{net imports}}{\text{gross available energy}}, \qquad \mathrm{HHI} = \sum_i (100\, s_i)^2$$

- **Symbols.** $s_i$ is supplier $i$'s share of a supply, from 0 to 1; the HHI runs from near 0 (many small suppliers) to 10,000 (one).
- **Equal shares.** With $n$ equal suppliers the HHI is $10{,}000/n$: four refiners can never bring it below 2,500.
- **Stock days.** The IEA counts oil stocks in days of the previous year's net imports, not of all oil used.
- **The scarcest input.** A factory needing several inputs makes as much as its scarcest input allows: a minimum, not an average.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Security inside a planning model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **An import-share cap.** A rule that imports stay below a share of primary energy in each period; its dual value prices that security.
- **Stocks as decisions.** A two-stage model chooses stock sizes before it knows which disruption comes, then runs each one.
- **Disruption scenarios.** Shocks become scenarios with stated settings, as on this page, so a plan can be tested against them.
- **Next.** Modeler lesson [M13](m13-national-pathway.html) adds an import-share cap to Prairieland's pathway model; capstone [C4](c4-prairieland-2050.html) tests a pathway against shocks.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>How prices, demand and trade respond during a shock, beyond the levers you set.</li>
<li>Shipping, insurance and the cost of holding and refreshing stocks.</li>
<li>Mining, refining and trade law, and any judgement of a country's policies.</li>
<li>Cybersecurity and the physical security of grids and plants.</li>
<li>The odds of any shock: these are stress tests, not forecasts.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 30 minutes: four myths, then six exercises with worked answers.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a21-myth">
<!-- a21-myths:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="independence" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A country that imports no energy is secure.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Risk also sits in world prices, single routes, dominant suppliers and single sites: Prairieland's coal is all domestic and all from one county.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="days" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Ninety days of oil stocks means ninety days of all the oil a country uses.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The IEA counts days of net imports: Prairieland's 60 days are 161.1 PJ, not 60 days of all its crude.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sellers" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “More LNG sellers protect a country from a world price spike.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A world price rise reaches every seller: Prairieland would still pay $8.40 billion more abroad, and only using less gas helps.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="hhi" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A high HHI shows that a supplier is likely to cut a country off.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It measures how concentrated supply is, not anyone's intentions; it says how much is at stake if one supplier stops.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- a21-myths:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-card a21-practice">
<!-- a21-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>Through the strait.</b> Prairieland imports 980 PJ of crude (all through the strait) and 420 PJ of LNG (25% through it). Primary energy is 3,500 PJ. What share passes the strait?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>980 + 420 × 0.25 = 1,085 PJ; ÷ 3,500 = 31.0%.</p></details></li><li><p><b>An HHI by hand.</b> Graphite's refiners hold 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%. What is the HHI?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>90² + 5² + 3² + 2² = 8,100 + 25 + 9 + 4 = 8,138.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Whose money.</b> LNG costs $10.00 per GJ and triples for a year; Prairieland buys 420 PJ. How much more does it pay abroad?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>420 PJ × $10.00 × (3 − 1) = $8,400 million, $8.40 billion.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Stocks against a closure.</b> With 60 days of stocks, does a 9-week closure leave Prairieland short? Oil imports are 980 PJ a year.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Lost: 980 × 63 ÷ 365 = 169.2 PJ; stocks: 980 × 60 ÷ 365 = 161.1 PJ; short by 8.1 PJ.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The scarcest mineral.</b> Country R refines 90% of graphite; 5% is recycled; stocks last 60 days. Over a 2-year restriction, what share of output can graphite support?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>5% + 95% × 10% = 14.5% a year; (2 × 0.145 + 60/365) ÷ 2 = 0.227, about 23%.</p></details></li><li><p><b>A second site.</b> The factory makes 12 GWh a year with 20 GWh of capacity. A fire stops the main site for 6 months. How much is lost with no second site, and with 30% of the capacity elsewhere?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>None elsewhere: 6/12 × 12 = 6.0 GWh. With 30%: 6/12 × (12 − 20 × 0.3) = 3.0 GWh.</p></details></li></ol><p class="lx-hint">Prairieland is fictional; its numbers are illustrative. Every number here comes from the page's model.</p>
<!-- a21-practice:end -->
</div>
```
